orig_9709_s1_norm_normal_areas.description: Read normal parameters correctly, interpret probabilities as areas, and standardise tails and intervals using an explicit cumulative-table convention.

sections.title: What do the parameters and the density curve represent?
sections.label: Continuous models
sections.intro:
For a normal model with positive standard deviation, write

\[X\sim\mathrm{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),\qquad\sigma>0.\]

The first parameter is the mean. The second is the variance, so the standard deviation is its nonnegative square root. The normal curve is symmetric about \(\mu\), where its mean, median and mode coincide.

The vertical axis is probability density. Probability is represented by area under the curve over an interval, and the total area is one. A density height alone is not a probability and need not lie between zero and one.

blocks.title: Stop and think: does a density height give a point probability?
blocks.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(40,25)\). Choose the correct interpretation of the density curve, then state the standard deviation and \(P(X=40)\).

fields.label: What represents probability on the curve?

options.area: Area over an interval represents probability; a height alone does not.
options.height: The height at forty is the probability of exactly forty.
options.peak: The whole probability is at the peak because forty is the mean.

fields.label: Probability of the exact value forty

blocks.hint: The second distribution parameter is a variance. A single point has zero horizontal width under a continuous density.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\sigma=\sqrt{25}=5,\qquad P(X=40)=0.\]

    Probabilities are density areas over events. A curve height is not a point mass.

blocks.html: Continuous endpoints have zero probability. For every specified real value \(a\), \(P(X=a)=0\). Therefore \(P(X<a)=P(X\le a)\), and changing strict to inclusive fixed endpoints leaves a normal interval probability unchanged.

A symmetric single-peaked shape is not proof of normality. Other continuous distributions can have those features. Use a normal model when it is stated or justified by the problem’s modelling assumptions, rather than inferring it from symmetry alone.

sections.title: How does the standard scale preserve the event area?
sections.label: Standardisation
sections.intro:
Subtracting the mean and dividing by the positive standard deviation expresses a value as a number of standard deviations from the mean:

\[Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,1).\]

A positive standardised value lies above the mean; a negative value lies below it. A value of zero is the mean itself. Use \(\sigma\), not the variance \(\sigma^2\), in the denominator.

blocks.html:
The two horizontal scales mark the same shaded event. The calculator gives \(\Phi(2)-\Phi(-1)\approx0.8186\). Four-decimal table entries give \(0.9772-0.1587=0.8185\).

Standardisation takes the original bounds eighty-five and one hundred thirty to minus one and two. The shaded probability stays the same; an unrounded normal calculation gives approximately 0.8186.

blocks.title: Translate known cutoffs in both directions
blocks.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(30,4^2)\) and \(Z=\frac{X-30}{4}\). Find the standardised values of twenty-two and thirty-six, then find the original-scale cutoff corresponding to \(Z=-0.5\).

fields.label: Original value corresponding to negative one half

blocks.hint: Subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation to go to the standard scale. Multiply by the standard deviation and add the mean to return.

blocks.html: Translate the whole event before looking up an area. Standardise both endpoints of an interval separately and keep the inequality direction. For reverse translation with known parameters, use \(X=\mu+\sigma Z\).

sections.title: Which area does the normal table actually report?
sections.label: Normal tables
sections.intro:
This lesson uses the lower cumulative convention

\[\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z),\qquad Z\sim\mathrm{N}(0,1).\]

Thus \(\Phi(0)=\frac{1}{2}\). Cumulative probabilities increase as their bound moves to the right. A positive bound has cumulative probability above one half; a negative bound has cumulative probability below one half.

blocks.title: Read a negative lower tail and a positive upper tail
blocks.prompt: Use the convention \(\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z)\) for \(Z\sim\mathrm{N}(0,1)\). Find \(P(Z\le-0.92)\) and \(P(Z>1.18)\), to four decimal places.
blocks.hint: A negative lower tail is the reflection of the matching positive upper tail. A positive upper tail is one minus its cumulative table entry.

blocks.html:
Rounding convention. Calculator answers in this lesson keep the cumulative values unrounded and round the final probability to four decimal places. A printed table may already round each cumulative entry to four decimal places. Subtracting or doubling those entries can change the final probability by \(0.0001\); the checks accept that table-rounding difference.

For example, the diagrammed interval \(-1<Z<2\) has unrounded probability approximately \(0.8185946\), giving \(0.8186\). A four-decimal-place table gives \(0.9772-0.1587=0.8185\). State or follow the supplied table convention, and avoid further rounding during the calculation.

Do not mix table conventions. A lower cumulative entry, an upper-tail entry and an area from zero to a positive bound describe different shaded regions. Inspect the heading or sketch before adding a half or subtracting from one.

sections.title: Which side of the boundary is the requested event?
sections.label: Normal tails
sections.intro:
With the lower cumulative convention, a right-tail probability is a complement:

\[P(Z>z)=1-\Phi(z).\]

Symmetry supplies negative bounds:

\[\Phi(-a)=1-\Phi(a).\]

For an original normal variable, standardise the boundary first, then choose the side requested by the original inequality.

blocks.title: Use the original units to identify the requested tail
blocks.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(80,16)\). Find \(P(X>85)\) and \(P(X<78)\), to four decimal places.
blocks.hint: The standard deviation is four. Standardise each boundary, then retain the direction of the original event.
blocks.solution:
1. \[P(X>85)=P\left(Z>\frac{85-80}{4}\right)=1-\Phi(1.25)\approx0.1056,\]
  2. \[P(X<78)=P\left(Z<\frac{78-80}{4}\right)=\Phi(-0.5)\approx0.3085.\]

blocks.html: Use the mean as a direction check. The area below a boundary above the mean is greater than one half. The area above that same boundary is less than one half. A sketch of the event helps catch an omitted complement even when the arithmetic is correct.

sections.title: Which cumulative areas leave the required interval?
sections.label: Intervals and symmetry
sections.intro:
For ordered standardised bounds \(a<b\),

\[P(a<Z<b)=\Phi(b)-\Phi(a).\]

The larger cumulative area includes everything to the left of \(b\). Subtracting the area left of \(a\) removes the unwanted lower region. This works whether the interval crosses zero or lies entirely on one side.

blocks.title: Subtract the two cumulative bounds of each interval
blocks.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(12,9)\). Find \(P(9.6<X<16.5)\) and \(P(12.6<X<15.6)\), to four decimal places. A four-decimal-place cumulative-table method is accepted under the stated rounding convention.

fields.label: Probability of the interval crossing the mean
Probability of the interval above the mean

blocks.hint: The standard deviation is three. The first standardised interval is from \(-0.8\) to \(1.5\); the second is from \(0.2\) to \(1.2\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[P(9.6<X<16.5)=\Phi(1.5)-\Phi(-0.8)\approx0.7213,\]
  2. \[P(12.6<X<15.6)=\Phi(1.2)-\Phi(0.2)\approx0.3057.\]

    Using four-decimal-place table entries for the second calculation gives \(0.8849-0.5793=0.3056\), which is also accepted as a table-rounding result.

blocks.html: The two tails beyond minus and plus one point five have equal areas, approximately 0.0668 each. Removing both leaves the central area, approximately 0.8664.

blocks.title: Translate an absolute deviation into a central interval
blocks.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(55,6^2)\). State the lower and upper endpoints of the event \(|X-55|\le12\), then find its probability and the probability \(P(|X-55|>12)\), to four decimal places.

fields.label: Lower endpoint of the central interval
Upper endpoint of the central interval

blocks.hint: The event is within two standard deviations of the mean. The outside event contains two equal tails.
blocks.solution:
1. \[|X-55|\le12\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad43\le X\le67\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad|Z|\le2.\]
  2. \[P(|Z|\le2)=2\Phi(2)-1\approx0.9545,\qquad P(|Z|>2)\approx0.0455.\]

  3. A four-decimal-place table with \(\Phi(2)\approx0.9772\) as its rounded entry gives \(0.9544\) and \(0.0456\). These are accepted table-rounding alternatives.

blocks.html:
For a positive \(a\), symmetry gives the useful central and outside forms

\[P(|Z|\le a)=2\Phi(a)-1,\qquad P(|Z|>a)=2[1-\Phi(a)].\]

For \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\), an absolute deviation \(|X-\mu|\le d\) corresponds to \(|Z|\le\frac{d}{\sigma}\). Write the two endpoints explicitly if the absolute-value wording is unfamiliar.

Check probability, event and precision together. An interval area is nonnegative and no larger than one. Central and outside areas add to one; symmetric opposite tails match. Report the requested side or interval and round only after the area calculation, according to the declared calculator or table method.

glossary.definition: A continuous model written \(\mathrm{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\), with positive standard deviation.
A curve whose area over an interval gives the probability of that interval.
The second parameter in normal notation; its square root is the standard deviation.
Subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation to express an event on the standard scale.
A normal variable with mean zero and variance one, written \(Z\sim\mathrm{N}(0,1)\).
The probability to the left of a bound, written \(\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z)\).
The probability to the right of a specified boundary.
The probability between two bounds equally distant from the mean.
Distance from the mean, allowing displacement in either direction.
The specific area represented by a published normal-table entry.

examples.title: Read the variance and interpret a continuous point event
examples.question: A measurement is modelled by \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(72,16)\). State its mean, variance and standard deviation. Find \(P(X=72)\) and \(P(X<72)\).
solution:
The second parameter is the variance:

\[\mu=72,\qquad\sigma^2=16,\qquad\sigma=\sqrt{16}=4.\]

A normal variable is continuous. A single exact value has no width and therefore no area under the density curve:

\[P(X=72)=0.\]

The normal curve is symmetric about its mean, so half its total area lies below seventy-two:

\[P(X<72)=\frac{1}{2}.\]

A reported rounded measurement is different from an exact point. For example, “72 to the nearest whole unit” represents the interval from 71.5 to 72.5, whose probability is an interval area. Zero probability at one specified point does not mean the continuous variable cannot realise a value.

examples.title: Standardise each endpoint using the standard deviation
examples.question: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(100,15^2)\). Translate \(85<X<130\) into an event for the standard normal variable \(Z\). Also translate the event \(Z\le0.8\) back into an event for \(X\).
solution:
The standard deviation is fifteen, so

\[Z=\frac{X-100}{15}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,1).\]

Transform the two original endpoints separately:

\[\frac{85-100}{15}=-1,\qquad\frac{130-100}{15}=2.\]

Since the divisor is positive, the inequality directions stay unchanged:

\[P(85<X<130)=P(-1<Z<2).\]

The probability is preserved; only the horizontal measurement units have changed.

For the reverse translation, use \(X=100+15Z\). Thus

\[Z\le0.8\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X\le100+15\cdot0.8=112.\]

The parameters are already known; this is a translation of an event between two scales.

examples.title: Read a cumulative table according to its stated area convention
examples.question:
A standard normal table reports \(\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z)\), rounded to four decimal places. Use the excerpt to find \(P(Z\le1.24)\). Explain why a different table might show \(0.3925\) for the same positive bound.

Row\(0.00\)\(0.01\)\(0.02\)\(0.03\)\(0.04\)
\(1.2\)\(0.8849\)\(0.8869\)\(0.8888\)\(0.8907\)\(0.8925\)
solution:
For \(z=1.24\), use row \(1.2\) and column \(0.04\). This cumulative table gives the whole area to the left:

\[P(Z\le1.24)=\Phi(1.24)\approx0.8925.\]

A table giving the area between zero and a positive bound would instead report

\[P(0<Z<1.24)=\Phi(1.24)-\frac{1}{2}\approx0.3925.\]

These are different areas of the same normal curve. To recover the cumulative probability from the second convention, add the left half:

\[\frac{1}{2}+0.3925=0.8925.\]
Read the heading or shaded diagram supplied with a table before deciding whether to use its entry directly, add one half, or take a complement.

examples.title: Use symmetry to read a negative standardised bound
examples.question: For \(Z\sim\mathrm{N}(0,1)\), find \(P(Z\le-0.73)\) and \(P(Z>-0.73)\), giving probabilities to four decimal places.
solution:
Reflection about zero turns the left tail below \(-0.73\) into the right tail above \(0.73\):

\[\Phi(-0.73)=1-\Phi(0.73).\]

The event to the right of the negative bound is its complement:

\[P(Z>-0.73)=1-\Phi(-0.73)=\Phi(0.73)\approx0.7673.\]
The negative bound lies left of the mean, so its left-tail probability is below one half and its right-tail probability is above one half. This gives a quick direction check.

examples.title: Match a measurement tail to the correct standard normal area
examples.question: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(48,2.5^2)\). Find \(P(X>52)\) and \(P(X<45)\), to four decimal places.
solution:
Use the standard deviation \(2.5\). The upper threshold is

\[z=\frac{52-48}{2.5}=1.6.\]

The requested area is to its right:

\[P(X>52)=P(Z>1.6)=1-\Phi(1.6)\approx0.0548.\]

The lower threshold is

\[z=\frac{45-48}{2.5}=-1.2.\]

The requested area is to its left:

\[P(X<45)=\Phi(-1.2)=1-\Phi(1.2)\approx0.1151.\]

Both requested regions are tails beyond a bound on their respective side of the mean, so both answers should be below one half. A cumulative-table entry above one half would need a complement for the first event.
Replacing \(>\) by \(\ge\), or \(<\) by \(\le\), does not change these normal probabilities because the probability at a single endpoint is zero.

examples.title: Subtract cumulative areas for intervals on either side of the mean
examples.question: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(60,25)\). Find \(P(55<X<67.5)\) and \(P(62.5<X<70)\), using unrounded normal calculations and giving final probabilities to four decimal places.
solution:
The variance is twenty-five, so the standard deviation is five. The first interval standardises to

\[\frac{55-60}{5}=-1,\qquad\frac{67.5-60}{5}=1.5.\]

\[P(55<X<67.5)=\Phi(1.5)-\Phi(-1)\approx0.7745.\]

Subtracting the left cumulative area through the lower bound leaves only the interval between the two bounds.

Both endpoints of the second interval are above the mean:

\[\frac{62.5-60}{5}=0.5,\qquad\frac{70-60}{5}=2.\]

The same cumulative subtraction works:

\[P(62.5<X<70)=\Phi(2)-\Phi(0.5)\approx0.2858.\]

Do not subtract the second interval from one merely because both bounds are positive. The event still asks for the area between them. A four-decimal-place cumulative table gives \(0.9772-0.6915=0.2857\); the one-unit difference in the final decimal comes from rounding those entries before subtraction.

examples.title: A central symmetric interval excludes two equal tails
examples.question: For \(Z\sim\mathrm{N}(0,1)\), find the probability in each tail beyond \(-1.5\) and \(1.5\), the central probability \(P(|Z|\le1.5)\), and the outside probability \(P(|Z|>1.5)\). Then express the central event for \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(20,4)\).
solution:
The two tail areas are equal:

\[P(Z>1.5)=P(Z<-1.5)=1-\Phi(1.5)\approx0.0668.\]

The central event is \(-1.5\le Z\le1.5\). Its probability is

\[P(|Z|\le1.5)=\Phi(1.5)-\Phi(-1.5)=2\Phi(1.5)-1\approx0.8664.\]

The outside event includes both disjoint tails:

\[P(|Z|>1.5)=2[1-\Phi(1.5)]\approx0.1336.\]

One tail alone is not the probability of being this far from the mean in either direction.

For \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(20,4)\), the standard deviation is two. Therefore

\[|Z|\le1.5\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad|X-20|\le3\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad17\le X\le23.\]

This interval has the same central probability \(0.8664\) to four decimal places.

extraPractice.title: Read the variance before standardising
extraPractice.prompt: A continuous duration \(X\), measured in minutes, is modelled by \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(34,16)\). State its standard deviation, standardise the value \(X=42\), find \(P(X=34)\), and select the correct interpretation of its density curve.

options.area: The probability of an interval is the area under the curve over that interval.
options.height: The height of the curve at a value equals the probability of that exact value.
options.variance: The second parameter in normal notation is the standard deviation.

extraPractice.hint: In \(\mathrm{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\), the second parameter is the variance. Divide the distance from the mean by the positive standard deviation. A single point has no interval width.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\mu=34,\qquad\sigma^2=16,\qquad\sigma=4.\]

    The standard deviation is four minutes.

  2. \[z=\frac{42-34}{4}=2.\]

    The denominator is the standard deviation, not the variance.

  3. Because the model is continuous, \(P(X=34)=0\), even though the curve is highest at its mean. Probabilities are areas over intervals; the density height is not a point probability.

extraPractice.title: Use a lower-cumulative table consistently
extraPractice.prompt:
Let \(Z\sim\mathrm{N}(0,1)\), with \(\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z)\). Find \(P(Z\le-0.67)\), \(P(Z>1.42)\), and \(P(-1.10<Z<0.35)\).

Give probabilities to four decimal places. Answers obtained from four-decimal lower-cumulative normal tables are accepted at table accuracy.
extraPractice.hint: Reflect a negative argument using \(\Phi(-a)=1-\Phi(a)\). An upper tail is one minus a lower-cumulative area. An interval is the upper cumulative area minus the lower cumulative area.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(Z\le-0.67)=1-\Phi(0.67)\approx0.2514.\]
  2. \[P(Z>1.42)=1-\Phi(1.42)\approx0.0778.\]
  3. \[P(-1.10<Z<0.35)=\Phi(0.35)-\Phi(-1.10)\approx0.5012.\]

    A four-decimal cumulative table gives \(0.6368-0.1357=0.5011\), which is also accepted at table accuracy. The interval crosses the mean, so it contains the area from each endpoint to the mean.

extraPractice.title: Strict endpoints do not change continuous areas
extraPractice.prompt:
The mass \(X\) of a component, in grams, has model \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(120,25)\). Find \(P(X<113)\), \(P(X\ge126)\), and \(P(113<X\le126)\).

Give probabilities to four decimal places. Answers obtained from four-decimal lower-cumulative normal tables are accepted at table accuracy.
extraPractice.hint: The standard deviation is five grams. Standardise both endpoints separately. Adding or removing an endpoint changes the event only by a singleton, which has probability zero.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\sigma=5,\qquad\frac{113-120}{5}=-1.40,\qquad\frac{126-120}{5}=1.20.\]
  2. \[P(X<113)=\Phi(-1.40)\approx0.0808,\]\[P(X\ge126)=1-\Phi(1.20)\approx0.1151.\]
  3. \[P(113<X\le126)=\Phi(1.20)-\Phi(-1.40)\approx0.8042.\]

    Using four-decimal table entries gives \(0.8849-0.0808=0.8041\), also valid at table accuracy. Since \(P(X=113)=P(X=126)=0\), changing strict to inclusive endpoints leaves these probabilities unchanged.

extraPractice.title: Reflect intervals about the mean
extraPractice.prompt:
Let \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(50,6.25)\). Find \(P(51.25<X<54)\), \(P(46<X<48.75)\), and \(P(50<X<51.25)\). Then compare the probabilities of \(50<X<51.25\) and \(51.25<X<52.5\), two intervals of equal width.

Give probabilities to four decimal places. Answers obtained from four-decimal lower-cumulative normal tables are accepted at table accuracy.

fields.label: Which equal-width interval has larger probability?

options.far: \(51.25<X<52.5\), the interval farther from the mean.
options.equal: They must be equal because their widths are equal.

extraPractice.hint: The standard deviation is \(2.5\). The first two intervals are mirror images about the mean. On the right of the mean, the density decreases as the distance from the mean increases.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\sigma=2.5,\qquad P(51.25<X<54)=P(0.50<Z<1.60)\]\[=\Phi(1.60)-\Phi(0.50)\approx0.2537.\]
  2. \[P(46<X<48.75)=P(-1.60<Z<-0.50)\approx0.2537.\]

    Reflection about the mean gives equal areas for these two intervals.

  3. \[P(50<X<51.25)=P(0<Z<0.50)=\Phi(0.50)-0.5\approx0.1915.\]

  4. The interval \(50<X<51.25\) has the larger probability. Both compared intervals have the same width, but every point in the nearer interval lies under a higher part of the normal density curve. Equal widths alone do not imply equal areas.

extraPractice.title: An absolute deviation includes both tails
extraPractice.prompt:
Let \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(10,4)\). Find \(P(|X-10|<3.5)\), \(P(|X-10|\ge3.5)\), and \(P(X\ge13.5)\).

Give probabilities to four decimal places. Answers obtained from four-decimal lower-cumulative normal tables are accepted at table accuracy.
extraPractice.hint: The standard deviation is two. The two boundary values are \(6.5\) and \(13.5\), at equal distances from the mean. An absolute deviation of at least \(3.5\) includes both outside tails.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[|X-10|<3.5\iff6.5<X<13.5\iff-1.75<Z<1.75.\]\[P(|X-10|<3.5)=1-2\cdot\Phi(-1.75)\approx0.9199.\]
  2. \[P(|X-10|\ge3.5)=2\cdot\Phi(-1.75)\approx0.0801,\]\[P(X\ge13.5)=\Phi(-1.75)\approx0.0401.\]

    The outside event has twice the probability of one tail. With a four-decimal cumulative table, the tail is \(0.0401\), giving outside probability \(0.0802\) and central probability \(0.9198\); both table results are accepted. Retain calculator precision if using a calculator.

starters.title: Filling limits and an accepted sub-interval
starters.question:
The amount \(X\) filled into a container, in millilitres, is modelled by \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(500,64)\). A container is accepted when \(488\le X\le510\). State the standard deviation. Find the probability of falling below the lower limit, the probability of exceeding the upper limit, and the probability of acceptance. Finally, find the probability that a randomly chosen container is accepted and its amount is below \(500\) millilitres.

Give probabilities to four decimal places. Answers obtained from four-decimal lower-cumulative normal tables are accepted at table accuracy.
starters.hint: Standardise both acceptance limits using the standard deviation. The final event is the part of the acceptance interval lying below the mean.
starters.solution:
1. \[\sigma=8,\qquad z_{\text{lower}}=\frac{488-500}{8}=-1.50,\qquad z_{\text{upper}}=\frac{510-500}{8}=1.25.\]
  2. \[P(X<488)=\Phi(-1.50)\approx0.0668,\]\[P(X>510)=1-\Phi(1.25)\approx0.1056.\]
  3. \[P(488\le X\le510)=\Phi(1.25)-\Phi(-1.50)\approx0.8275.\]

    The interval extends farther below the mean than above it. A four-decimal cumulative table gives \(0.8944-0.0668=0.8276\), also accepted.

  4. Being accepted and below the mean is the single interval \(488\le X<500\). Its probability is

    \[P(488\le X<500)=0.5-\Phi(-1.50)\approx0.4332.\]

    This is a part of the whole acceptance area. It is larger than the accepted area above the mean because the lower limit is farther from the mean than the upper limit.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: interpret the second parameter as variance and obtain the standard deviation.
  • 1 mark: standardise the lower acceptance limit.
  • 1 mark: standardise the upper acceptance limit.
  • 1 mark: obtain the lower-tail probability.
  • 1 mark: obtain the upper-tail probability using a complement.
  • 1 mark: subtract the cumulative areas in the correct order for acceptance.
  • 1 mark: give the acceptance probability at the stated accuracy.
  • 1 mark: identify the accepted-and-below-mean interval.
  • 1 mark: obtain its area by subtracting the lower tail from one half.
  • 1 mark: give that interval probability at the stated accuracy.

starters.title: Length bands and distance from a target
starters.question:
The length \(L\) of a cut strip, in centimetres, has model \(L\sim\mathrm{N}(30,2.25)\). Find the probability that a strip is shorter than \(28.8\) centimetres, the probability that \(28.8\le L\le31.95\), the probability that its distance from the target length of \(30\) centimetres is at least \(1.95\) centimetres, and the probability that \(31.95<L<33\).

Give probabilities to four decimal places. Answers obtained from four-decimal lower-cumulative normal tables are accepted at table accuracy.
starters.hint: The standard deviation is \(1.5\) centimetres. Standardise each boundary separately. Distance from the target is a two-sided event, while the final interval lies wholly above the mean.
starters.solution:
1. \[\sigma=1.5,\qquad\frac{28.8-30}{1.5}=-0.80,\qquad\frac{31.95-30}{1.5}=1.30,\qquad\frac{33-30}{1.5}=2.00.\]
  2. \[P(L<28.8)=\Phi(-0.80)\approx0.2119.\]
  3. \[P(28.8\le L\le31.95)=\Phi(1.30)-\Phi(-0.80)\approx0.6913.\]

  4. The distance condition is \(L\le28.05\) or \(L\ge31.95\), which standardises to \(Z\le-1.30\) or \(Z\ge1.30\). Hence

    \[P(|L-30|\ge1.95)=2\cdot[1-\Phi(1.30)]\approx0.1936.\]
  5. \[P(31.95<L<33)=\Phi(2.00)-\Phi(1.30)\approx0.0741.\]

    The two cumulative areas are subtracted even though both endpoints are on the same side of the mean. Four-decimal table entries give \(0.9772-0.9032=0.0740\), also accepted at table accuracy.

revision.body:
Read the parameters, standardise the boundaries and identify the required area before using a normal table.

Notation and continuous probability

\[X\sim\mathrm{N}(\mu,\sigma^2),\qquad\sigma>0.\]

The parameters are the mean and variance. The standard deviation is the positive square root of the variance. Probabilities are areas under the density curve, whose total area is one. Curve height is not point probability. For every real \(a\), \(P(X=a)=0\), so changing a strict endpoint to an inclusive one leaves the probability unchanged.

Convert each boundary to a standard score

\[Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\sim\mathrm{N}(0,1),\qquad z_a=\frac{a-\mu}{\sigma}.\]

The mean maps to zero; values above it have positive standard scores and values below it have negative scores. Use the standard deviation in the denominator. For an interval, convert both boundaries. Since \(\sigma>0\), standardisation preserves the direction of each inequality.

Lower-cumulative tables, negatives and tails

\[\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z),\qquad\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z).\]\[P(Z>z)=1-\Phi(z).\]

Read the table’s convention first. A lower-cumulative table gives the whole area to the left. If a table instead gives the area from zero to a positive \(z\), add one half to obtain \(\Phi(z)\). Sketch the tail so that its side agrees with the event.

Subtract intervals and use reflection

\[P(a<X<b)=\Phi(z_b)-\Phi(z_a).\]\[P(|Z|<c)=2\cdot\Phi(c)-1\qquad(c>0).\]

Subtract the lower cumulative area from the upper, including when both boundaries lie on the same side of the mean. Reflected intervals have equal areas; equal widths alone do not guarantee this. Keep calculator precision until final rounding. Combining four-decimal table entries can change the last reported decimal, so use the stated table accuracy.
revision.checks: • Variance identified; positive standard deviation; both boundaries standardised; sign checked; table convention read; correct tail or interval shaded; cumulative areas subtracted in order; final rounding.
revision.examTip: Show each method, retain the required precision and state the complete answer.

orig_9709_s1_norm_inverse_normal.description: Convert tail probabilities into quantiles, find percentiles and central intervals, and recover normal parameters with explicit precision and consistency checks.

sections.title: Which lower cumulative probability corresponds to the requested cutoff?
sections.label: Inverse tails
sections.intro:
A direct normal calculation starts with a bound and finds an area. An inverse calculation starts with a cumulative area and finds the bound. For \(0<\alpha<1\), define

\[z_\alpha=\Phi^{-1}(\alpha),\qquad P(Z\le z_\alpha)=\alpha.\]

The inverse symbol means the inverse function, not a reciprocal. An upper-tail probability \(u\) must first be converted to lower cumulative probability \(1-u\).

blocks.html: The lower 10% cutoff is approximately minus 1.282; the upper 10% cutoff is approximately plus 1.282 and is the 90th percentile. The probability passed to the inverse is the area to the left.

blocks.title: Stop and think: which cumulative probability belongs in the inverse?
blocks.prompt: For a standard normal variable, \(P(Z>k)=0.15\). State the lower cumulative probability to use, choose the sign of \(k\), and find \(k\) to three decimal places. For a table method, use \(z_{0.85}\approx1.036\).

options.positive: Positive: the cutoff lies above zero.
options.zero: Zero: every tail percentage gives the median.

fields.label: Standardised cutoff to three decimal places

blocks.hint: The complement of the upper 15% is the lower 85%. A lower cumulative area above one half corresponds to a positive standardised value.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\Phi(k)=1-0.15=0.85,\qquad k=\Phi^{-1}(0.85)\approx1.036.\]

    The 15% upper tail begins at the 85th percentile.

blocks.html: Check the sign on the standard scale. A lower cumulative probability below \(0.5\) has a negative quantile; above \(0.5\) it has a positive quantile; exactly \(0.5\) gives zero. This sign refers to the standardised value, not necessarily the sign of the original measurement.

A nondegenerate normal distribution has no finite cutoff with cumulative probability exactly zero or one. Those are limiting tail probabilities as the cutoff tends to negative or positive infinity. Do not replace an endpoint inverse request by an arbitrary large finite number.

Precision convention. Use unrounded calculator inverse values where available, or the explicitly supplied three-decimal-place quantiles for a table method. Standardised answers are requested to three decimal places; original-scale values and parameters are normally requested to two. Checks accept the answers produced by both stated methods. Do not silently round the supplied quantiles further to two decimal places.

sections.title: What value has the stated proportion below it?
sections.label: Percentiles
sections.intro:
The \(100\alpha\)th percentile of \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\), with \(\sigma>0\), is the value \(x_\alpha\) satisfying \(P(X\le x_\alpha)=\alpha\). Standardising and rearranging gives

\[x_\alpha=\mu+\sigma z_\alpha.\]

A percentile is a measurement value. Its defining cumulative probability concerns the area below that value; the probability at one exact value remains zero.

blocks.title: Locate percentiles below and above a known median
blocks.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(70,6^2)\). Find its 20th and 80th percentiles to two decimal places, and state its median. For a table method, use \(z_{0.20}\approx-0.842\) and \(z_{0.80}\approx0.842\).
blocks.hint: Use \(x_\alpha=\mu+\sigma z_\alpha\). Symmetric percentile levels have cutoffs equally far from the mean.
blocks.solution:
1. \[x_{0.20}=70+6z_{0.20}\approx64.95,\qquad x_{0.80}=70+6z_{0.80}\approx75.05.\]

  2. The median is the mean, seventy. The supplied three-decimal-place quantiles give the same two-decimal-place answers here.

blocks.html: Use the requested percentile level as a lower cumulative probability. The 25th percentile has 25% below it and 75% above it. The median is the 50th percentile and equals the normal mean. Higher percentile levels must give larger original-scale cutoffs.

sections.title: How is a central probability divided between the two tails?
sections.label: Symmetric intervals
sections.intro:
If a symmetric central interval contains probability \(c\), its total outside probability is \(1-c\), so each tail contains \(\frac{1-c}{2}\). The cumulative probability at the upper endpoint is

\[1-\frac{1-c}{2}=\frac{1+c}{2}.\]

With \(z=z_{\frac{1+c}{2}}\), the original-scale central endpoints are

\[\mu-\sigma z,\qquad\mu+\sigma z.\]

Do not put the central probability \(c\) itself into the inverse as though it were the upper endpoint’s cumulative area.

blocks.title: Split the missing area in a symmetric central interval
blocks.prompt: Find the symmetric central 80% interval for \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(10,16)\). State the probability in each outside tail, then report both endpoints to two decimal places. For a table method, use \(z_{0.90}\approx1.282\).
blocks.hint: The total outside probability is 20%, so each tail has 10%. The standard deviation is four, and the upper cumulative probability is 90%.
blocks.solution:
1. \[a=10-4z_{0.90}\approx4.87,\qquad b=10+4z_{0.90}\approx15.13.\]

    The interval is approximately from \(4.87\) to \(15.13\), with one tenth in each outside tail before endpoint rounding.

blocks.html: Distinguish the central mass from a one-sided percentile. A central 90% interval leaves 5% in each tail and uses the 95th-percentile upper bound. Using the 90th percentile would instead leave 10% above that bound.

sections.title: Which parameter is unknown in the standardised equation?
sections.label: One unknown
sections.intro:
A supplied condition \(P(X\le a)=\alpha\) gives the exact quantile equation

\[\frac{a-\mu}{\sigma}=z_\alpha.\]

If \(\sigma\) is known, solve \(\mu=a-\sigma z_\alpha\). If \(\mu\) is known and \(z_\alpha\ne0\), solve \(\sigma=\frac{a-\mu}{z_\alpha}\), then check that the result is positive. A supplied variance must first be square-rooted to obtain the standard deviation used here.

blocks.title: Solve a mean equation with the correct quantile sign
blocks.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(\mu,9)\), and suppose \(P(X\le21)=0.80\). Find \(\mu\) to two decimal places, and state whether the cutoff twenty-one lies above or below the mean. For a table method, use \(z_{0.80}\approx0.842\).
blocks.hint: The standard deviation is three. The 80th percentile has a positive standardised value, so \(21-\mu\) must be positive.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\mu=21-3z_{0.80}\approx18.47513630\approx18.48.\]

  2. The supplied table value gives \(\mu\approx21-3\cdot0.842=18.474\), or \(18.47\) to two decimal places; that stated-method answer is also accepted. In either case, twenty-one lies above the mean.

blocks.title: A known median does not identify the spread
blocks.prompt: A normal variable has known mean forty and satisfies \(P(X<37)=0.10\). Find its positive standard deviation to two decimal places. For a table method, use \(z_{0.10}\approx-1.282\). Separately, if the only supplied probability were \(P(X\le40)=0.50\), would that determine the standard deviation?

fields.label: Does the median-only condition determine the spread?

options.no: No: it holds for every positive standard deviation with this mean.
options.yes: Yes: the standard deviation must be zero.
options.impossible: No: a normal model cannot have half its area below its mean.

blocks.hint: For the first condition, both the numerator and standardised quantile are negative. For the separate median condition, the standardised value is zero regardless of the positive spread.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\frac{37-40}{\sigma}=z_{0.10},\qquad\sigma=\frac{-3}{z_{0.10}}\approx2.34.\]

  2. The median-only statement supplies no new information about \(\sigma\): \(P(X\le40)=0.5\) for every positive standard deviation when the mean is forty.

blocks.html: A median condition can leave the spread undetermined. If the mean is known and \(\alpha=0.5\), then \(z_\alpha=0\). A cutoff equal to the mean is compatible with every positive standard deviation; a different claimed median is inconsistent. Division by the zero quantile does not recover a spread.

Check the sign before reporting a standard deviation. The original displacement and its standardised quantile must have the same sign. If the calculation gives a negative spread, recheck the tail conversion and data; taking an absolute value without justification does not repair inconsistent percentile information.

sections.title: Do the two distinct percentile constraints identify one valid normal model?
sections.label: Two unknowns
sections.intro:
For distinct cumulative levels \(0<\alpha<\beta<1\), suppose \(a\) and \(b\) are the corresponding percentile values. The two equations are

\[a=\mu+\sigma z_\alpha,\qquad b=\mu+\sigma z_\beta.\]

Subtract them to eliminate the mean:

\[\sigma=\frac{b-a}{z_\beta-z_\alpha},\qquad\mu=a-\sigma z_\alpha.\]

Because \(z_\beta>z_\alpha\), a valid positive standard deviation requires \(b>a\). Keep quantile precision through the subtraction and division, then back-substitute both original conditions.

blocks.html: The symmetric 10th and 90th percentiles forty and sixty put the mean exactly at fifty. Using the supplied quantiles approximately minus and plus 1.282 gives a standard deviation approximately 7.80; a full-precision inverse gives approximately 7.8030.

blocks.title: Recover two parameters and reject reversed percentile ordering
blocks.prompt: A normal variable has 20th percentile thirty-eight and 80th percentile fifty. Find its mean and standard deviation, giving the standard deviation to two decimal places. Use \(z_{0.20}\approx-0.842\) and \(z_{0.80}\approx0.842\) for a table method. A separate proposal reverses these cutoffs, claiming 20th percentile fifty and 80th percentile thirty-eight. Is that proposal admissible?

options.inconsistent: Inconsistent: a higher percentile cannot have a smaller cutoff.
options.valid: Valid: use a negative standard deviation.
options.underdetermined: Underdetermined: there are too few distinct percentile levels.

blocks.hint: The first pair is symmetric about the mean. Subtract the two quantile equations to obtain the positive spread; then check the separate proposal’s ordering.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\mu=\frac{38+50}{2}=44,\qquad\sigma=\frac{50-38}{z_{0.80}-z_{0.20}}=\frac{6}{z_{0.80}}\approx7.13.\]

  2. The supplied table quantiles also give \(\sigma\approx\frac{12}{1.684}\approx7.13\). Reversing the cutoffs reverses the required order and would produce a negative standard deviation, so the separate proposal is inconsistent.

blocks.html: Equal and inconsistent constraints. Repeating the same percentile level at the same cutoff merely repeats one equation and does not identify both parameters. Giving the same exact percentile level at two different cutoffs is inconsistent with a strictly increasing normal cumulative distribution. Giving two distinct percentile levels at the same cutoff would force zero spread, outside the positive-standard-deviation model. Reversing the order of two distinct percentile cutoffs is also inconsistent.

Check the model notation after solving. In \(\mathrm{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\), the second parameter is the variance. If the requested output is a variance, square the unrounded recovered standard deviation and then round; do not insert the standard deviation directly into the variance position.

Back-substitute before rounding away the evidence. Recover the original standardised bounds from the unrounded parameters and check their cumulative levels and order. When working with the supplied rounded table quantiles, use approximation signs and judge agreement at that stated precision.

glossary.definition: A cutoff having a specified cumulative probability below it.
Finding a normal cutoff from a lower cumulative probability.
An original-scale cutoff identified by the percentage of the distribution below it.
A cutoff with a stated probability above it; its inverse input is the complementary lower cumulative probability.
An interval symmetric about the mean with the stated probability between its endpoints.
The relation \(a=\mu+\sigma z_\alpha\) for a percentile cutoff.
The requirement that a nondegenerate normal model has standard deviation strictly greater than zero.
Conditions that do not provide enough distinct information to recover both parameters uniquely.
The requirement that a higher cumulative percentile has a larger cutoff in a positive-spread normal model.
Checking recovered parameters in the original percentile equations before final rounding.

examples.title: An upper-tail percentage uses the complementary lower cumulative area
examples.question: For \(Z\sim\mathrm{N}(0,1)\), find the cutoff containing 10% of the distribution below it, and the cutoff containing 10% above it. Give standardised cutoffs to three decimal places. For a table method, use \(z_{0.10}\approx-1.282\) and \(z_{0.90}\approx1.282\).
solution:
The lower-tail cutoff \(a\) satisfies

\[P(Z\le a)=0.10,\qquad a=\Phi^{-1}(0.10)\approx-1.282.\]

A cumulative area below one half requires a cutoff below zero.

The upper-tail cutoff \(b\) has \(P(Z>b)=0.10\). Convert this to the lower cumulative area before using the inverse:

\[P(Z\le b)=0.90,\qquad b=\Phi^{-1}(0.90)\approx1.282.\]
The upper 10% begins above the 90th percentile. It does not begin at the 10th percentile, which is on the opposite side of the mean.
The two cutoffs have equal magnitudes and opposite signs because the two tail areas are equal. The displayed values are rounded approximations to the exact quantiles.

examples.title: Transform a standard normal upper-tail cutoff to original units
examples.question: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(80,12^2)\). Find the value \(c\) exceeded by the upper 5% of values, to two decimal places. For a table method, use \(z_{0.95}\approx1.645\).
solution:
The requested condition is \(P(X>c)=0.05\), so \(P(X\le c)=0.95\). Its standardised cutoff is

\[z_{0.95}=\Phi^{-1}(0.95)\approx1.644853627.\]

Translate back with the known mean and standard deviation:

\[c=80+12z_{0.95}\approx99.73824352.\]
The answer is \(c\approx99.74\). Using the supplied three-decimal-place quantile gives \(c\approx80+12\cdot1.645=99.74\), the same reported answer.
The cutoff is above the mean, as an upper 5% threshold must be. Dividing by the standard deviation here would reverse the original-scale transformation.

examples.title: A percentile is an original-scale value, not a point probability
examples.question: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(64,8^2)\). Find its 25th percentile and median, and interpret both. Give the percentile to two decimal places. For a table method, use \(z_{0.25}\approx-0.674\).
solution:
The 25th-percentile value \(x_{0.25}\) has cumulative probability \(0.25\). Hence

\[x_{0.25}=64+8z_{0.25}.\]

An unrounded inverse normal calculation gives \(z_{0.25}\approx-0.674489750\), so

\[x_{0.25}\approx58.60408200\approx58.60\quad\text{(2 decimal places)}.\]

The supplied table approximation gives \(x_{0.25}\approx64+8\cdot(-0.674)=58.608\), or \(58.61\) to two decimal places. This small method-dependent difference is accepted when the supplied three-decimal-place quantile is used.

The median corresponds to cumulative probability \(0.5\), for which \(z_{0.5}=0\). Thus the median is exactly \(64\). Approximately 25% lie below the reported lower-quartile cutoff, and half lie below the median. Neither statement assigns positive probability to one exact point.

examples.title: Split the outside mass before finding a central interval
examples.question: Find the symmetric central 90% interval for \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(30,4^2)\). Give the endpoints to two decimal places. For a table method, use \(z_{0.95}\approx1.645\).
solution: The total outside probability is \(0.10\). Symmetry puts \(0.05\) in each tail, so the lower and upper cumulative probabilities are \(0.05\) and \(0.95\).

The standardised bounds are \(-z_{0.95}\) and \(z_{0.95}\), not the 10th and 90th percentiles. Therefore

\[a=30-4z_{0.95},\qquad b=30+4z_{0.95}.\]

Using an unrounded inverse gives \(a\approx23.42058549\) and \(b\approx36.57941451\). The central interval is

\[23.42<X<36.58\quad\text{(endpoints to 2 decimal places)}.\]

The supplied \(1.645\) gives the same two-decimal-place endpoints. The exact unrounded interval has probability \(0.90\); reporting rounded endpoints gives a correspondingly approximate interval. “Central” specifies symmetry—other nonsymmetric intervals can also contain 90% of a normal distribution.

examples.title: Recover an unknown mean from a known standard deviation
examples.question: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(\mu,25)\), and suppose \(P(X<24)=0.10\). Find \(\mu\) to two decimal places. For a table method, use \(z_{0.10}\approx-1.282\).
solution:
The known variance is twenty-five, so \(\sigma=5\). The exact quantile equation is

\[\frac{24-\mu}{5}=z_{0.10}.\]

Rearrange for the mean:

\[\mu=24-5z_{0.10}.\]

Using an unrounded inverse normal value gives

\[\mu\approx30.40775783\approx30.41.\]
With the supplied table quantile, \(\mu\approx24-5\cdot(-1.282)=30.41\), giving the same reported answer.
The 10th percentile must lie below the mean. The recovered mean is indeed above twenty-four. Using a positive standardised value for the lower 10% would place the mean on the wrong side.

examples.title: Recover a positive standard deviation and then the variance
examples.question: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(50,\sigma^2)\), with \(\sigma>0\), and suppose \(P(X>62)=0.025\). Find the standard deviation and variance to two decimal places. For a table method, use \(z_{0.975}\approx1.960\).
solution:
Convert the upper-tail probability to a lower cumulative probability:

\[P(X\le62)=0.975,\qquad\frac{62-50}{\sigma}=z_{0.975}.\]

The cutoff is above the mean, so its positive standardised value is consistent with a positive standard deviation:

\[\sigma=\frac{12}{z_{0.975}}\approx6.122561483\approx6.12.\]

Keep the unrounded standard deviation when finding the variance:

\[\sigma^2=\frac{144}{z_{0.975}^2}\approx37.48575911\approx37.49.\]

Thus a calculator-based reported model is approximately \(\mathrm{N}(50,37.49)\). Its second parameter is a variance, not the reported standard deviation \(6.12\).

The supplied table value gives \(\sigma\approx6.122448980\) and \(\sigma^2\approx37.48438151\), reporting \(6.12\) and \(37.48\). Both stated methods are valid at their declared quantile precision. Squaring the already rounded \(6.12\) would introduce an additional avoidable error.

examples.title: Use two percentile equations and verify their order
examples.question: A normal variable has 10th percentile forty and 90th percentile sixty. Find its mean and standard deviation, giving the standard deviation to two decimal places. For a table method, use \(z_{0.10}\approx-1.282\) and \(z_{0.90}\approx1.282\).
solution:
Each original-scale percentile supplies one equation:

\[40=\mu+\sigma z_{0.10},\qquad60=\mu+\sigma z_{0.90}.\]

The 10th and 90th percentiles are symmetric, with \(z_{0.10}=-z_{0.90}\). Adding the exact equations gives

\[100=2\mu,\qquad\mu=50.\]

Subtracting the equations gives

\[20=\sigma(z_{0.90}-z_{0.10})=2\sigma z_{0.90},\qquad\sigma=\frac{10}{z_{0.90}}.\]

The unrounded inverse gives \(\sigma\approx7.803041461\), so \(\sigma\approx7.80\) to two decimal places.

Using the supplied quantiles gives the approximate equations

\[40\approx\mu-1.282\sigma,\qquad60\approx\mu+1.282\sigma,\]\[\sigma\approx\frac{20}{2.564}\approx7.800312012.\]

This also reports \(7.80\). The approximation signs matter because the displayed standardised quantiles are rounded.

Back-substitution with the unrounded recovered parameters returns standardised bounds approximately \(-1.281551566\) and \(1.281551566\), with cumulative probabilities \(0.10\) and \(0.90\). The larger percentile has the larger value and the standard deviation is positive.

extraPractice.title: Convert the stated tail before finding the cutoff
extraPractice.prompt:
A duration \(X\), in seconds, has model \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(80,36)\). Find \(b\) such that \(P(X>b)=0.15\), and \(a\) such that \(P(X<a)=0.08\). Then decide whether cumulative probabilities zero or one have finite real cutoffs in this model. Supplied quantiles: \(z_{0.85}\approx1.036\), \(z_{0.08}\approx-1.405\).

Give cutoffs and unknown parameters to two decimal places unless an exact answer is requested. You may use a calculator or the supplied three-decimal standard-normal quantiles, where \(P(Z\le z_q)=q\). Retain your chosen quantiles and inferred parameters until final rounding; answers at the supplied-value accuracy are accepted.

fields.label: Finite cutoffs for cumulative probabilities zero and one

options.neither: Neither probability has a finite real cutoff.
options.zero: Only cumulative probability zero has a finite real cutoff.
options.one: Only cumulative probability one has a finite real cutoff.
options.both: Both probabilities have finite real cutoffs.

extraPractice.hint: The standard deviation is six seconds. An upper-tail probability of \(0.15\) means a lower-cumulative probability of \(0.85\). Normal tails approach zero but remain positive beyond every finite cutoff.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(X\le b)=0.85,\qquad b=80+6\cdot z_{0.85}\approx86.22.\]

    The cutoff is above the mean because its lower-cumulative probability exceeds one half.

  2. \[a=80+6\cdot z_{0.08}\approx71.57.\]

    This cutoff is below the mean. The supplied quantiles give the same two-decimal answers.

  3. For every finite real \(x\), a nondegenerate normal model satisfies \(0<P(X\le x)<1\). Thus neither zero nor one has a finite real quantile. These probabilities occur only as limiting cumulative areas as the cutoff moves without bound.

extraPractice.title: Percentiles and an interquartile width
extraPractice.prompt:
The length \(L\) of a rod, in millimetres, is modelled by \(L\sim\mathrm{N}(50,16)\). Find its 90th percentile, its lower quartile, and its interquartile range. Supplied quantiles: \(z_{0.90}\approx1.282\), \(z_{0.25}\approx-0.674\), \(z_{0.75}\approx0.674\).

Give cutoffs and unknown parameters to two decimal places unless an exact answer is requested. You may use a calculator or the supplied three-decimal standard-normal quantiles, where \(P(Z\le z_q)=q\). Retain your chosen quantiles and inferred parameters until final rounding; answers at the supplied-value accuracy are accepted.
extraPractice.hint: A percentile is a lower-cumulative area. The lower and upper quartiles use cumulative probabilities \(0.25\) and \(0.75\). The interquartile range is the difference between their values.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\sigma=4,\qquad x_{0.90}=50+4\cdot z_{0.90}\approx55.13.\]
  2. \[Q_1=50+4\cdot z_{0.25}\approx47.30.\]

    The negative lower-quartile standard score places it below the mean.

  3. \[Q_3-Q_1=4\cdot(z_{0.75}-z_{0.25})\approx5.40.\]

    Using the supplied three-decimal quantiles instead gives \(4\cdot(0.674+0.674)=5.392\), which rounds to \(5.39\) and is accepted at the supplied-value accuracy. Subtract unrounded quartiles or use the unrounded standard-score difference.

extraPractice.title: Split the omitted mass into two equal tails
extraPractice.prompt:
Let \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(42,9)\). Find the probability in each tail outside the central \(92\%\) interval, and the lower and upper endpoints of that central interval. Give the tail probability exactly. The interval is symmetric about the mean. Supplied quantile: \(z_{0.96}\approx1.751\).

Give cutoffs and unknown parameters to two decimal places unless an exact answer is requested. You may use a calculator or the supplied three-decimal standard-normal quantiles, where \(P(Z\le z_q)=q\). Retain your chosen quantiles and inferred parameters until final rounding; answers at the supplied-value accuracy are accepted.
extraPractice.hint: The total probability outside is \(0.08\), shared equally between the two tails. The upper endpoint therefore has cumulative probability \(0.96\), rather than \(0.92\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(\text{each tail})=\frac{1-0.92}{2}=0.04=\frac{1}{25}.\]
  2. \[\sigma=3,\qquad x_{\text{lower}}=42-3\cdot z_{0.96}\approx36.75,\]\[x_{\text{upper}}=42+3\cdot z_{0.96}\approx47.25.\]

    The endpoints lie at equal distances from the mean. The supplied quantile gives the same rounded endpoints.

extraPractice.title: Solve separate models with one unknown parameter
extraPractice.prompt:
Consider two separate normal models. For \(X\), the variance is \(25\) and \(P(X>73)=0.10\); find its mean. For \(Y\), the mean is \(20\) and \(P(Y<17)=0.20\); find its standard deviation and variance. Supplied quantiles: \(z_{0.90}\approx1.282\), \(z_{0.20}\approx-0.842\).

Give cutoffs and unknown parameters to two decimal places unless an exact answer is requested. You may use a calculator or the supplied three-decimal standard-normal quantiles, where \(P(Z\le z_q)=q\). Retain your chosen quantiles and inferred parameters until final rounding; answers at the supplied-value accuracy are accepted.
extraPractice.hint: In the first model, convert the upper tail to cumulative probability \(0.90\) and use standard deviation five. In the second, both the cutoff-minus-mean and its standard score are negative, producing a positive standard deviation.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[73=\mu_X+5\cdot z_{0.90},\qquad\mu_X=73-5\cdot z_{0.90}\approx66.59.\]
  2. \[\frac{17-20}{\sigma_Y}=z_{0.20},\qquad\sigma_Y=\frac{-3}{z_{0.20}}\approx3.56.\]

    The positive result is consistent with a lower-tail cutoff below the mean.

  3. \[\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\left(\frac{-3}{z_{0.20}}\right)^2\approx12.71.\]

    Using the supplied standard score gives \(\sigma_Y=\frac{3}{0.842}\) and variance approximately \(12.69458\), which rounds to \(12.69\) and is accepted. Quantile rounding is amplified by the division and squaring. Do not square the already rounded value \(3.56\).

extraPractice.title: Decide whether percentile information determines a valid model
extraPractice.prompt:
Each record is a separate claim about a normal model \(\mathrm{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma>0\). Classify each record as determining one valid model, allowing more than one valid model, or being inconsistent.

A: the 25th percentile is \(20\), and the 75th percentile is \(28\).

B: the 20th percentile is \(20\), and the 80th percentile is \(16\).

C: \(P(X<10)=0.30\) and \(P(X>10)=0.70\).

D: both the 40th percentile and the 60th percentile are \(8\).
extraPractice.hint: For positive standard deviation, increasing cumulative probabilities require strictly increasing percentile values. Complementary statements about the same cutoff may provide the same equation twice.
extraPractice.solution:
1. A determines one valid model. Normal symmetry fixes the mean at the midpoint \(24\); the positive interquartile width determines one positive standard deviation.

  2. B is inconsistent. The 80th percentile must exceed the 20th percentile, whereas the recorded values are in decreasing order. Solving the two equations would produce a negative standard deviation.

  3. C is underdetermined. Since a normal singleton has probability zero, the two displayed events are complementary and supply the same information. Each positive standard deviation can be paired with a suitable mean to place the 30th percentile at \(10\).

  4. D is inconsistent. A strictly increasing normal cumulative distribution cannot give two different percentile probabilities at the same value. The corresponding linear equations would force \(\sigma=0\), which is excluded.

extraPractice.title: Find the median quantile
extraPractice.prompt: Find the standard normal z-value with lower-tail probability \(0.5\).
extraPractice.hint: The distribution is symmetric about zero.
extraPractice.solution:
The distribution is symmetric about zero.

  • Answer: \(0\)

extraPractice.title: Recover the mean
extraPractice.prompt: A normal variable has standard deviation \(4\). Its value \(54\) has the same cumulative probability as the standard normal value \(1.5\). Find its mean.
extraPractice.hint: The value is one and a half standard deviations above the mean.
extraPractice.solution:
The value is one and a half standard deviations above the mean.

  • Answer: \(48\)

extraPractice.title: Recover the positive spread
extraPractice.prompt: A normal variable has mean \(50\). Its value \(56\) has the same cumulative probability as the standard normal value \(1.5\). Find its standard deviation.
extraPractice.hint: Six units equal one and a half standard deviations.
extraPractice.solution:
Six units equal one and a half standard deviations.

  • Answer: \(4\)

extraPractice.title: Use two quantiles
extraPractice.prompt: The values \(41\) and \(65\) correspond to z-scores \(-1.5\) and \(1.5\). Find the mean and standard deviation.
extraPractice.hint: The two values lie symmetrically about the mean, and their separation is three standard deviations.
extraPractice.solution:
The two values lie symmetrically about the mean, and their separation is three standard deviations.

  • Mean: \(53\)
  • Standard deviation: \(8\)

starters.title: Two percentiles determine the mean and scale
starters.question:
The mass \(X\) of a packet, in grams, has a normal model with unknown mean \(\mu\) and positive standard deviation \(\sigma\). It is known that \(P(X\le95)=0.10\) and \(P(X\le107)=0.75\). Find \(\sigma\), \(\mu\) and the variance. Then find the mass exceeded by only \(5\%\) of packets, and the exact probability that \(95<X<107\). Show in your working that the inferred standard deviation is positive and the percentile order is consistent. Supplied quantiles: \(z_{0.10}\approx-1.282\), \(z_{0.75}\approx0.674\), \(z_{0.95}\approx1.645\).

Give cutoffs and unknown parameters to two decimal places unless an exact answer is requested. You may use a calculator or the supplied three-decimal standard-normal quantiles, where \(P(Z\le z_q)=q\). Retain your chosen quantiles and inferred parameters until final rounding; answers at the supplied-value accuracy are accepted.
starters.hint: Pair each measured cutoff with its own lower-cumulative standard score. Subtract the two equations to remove the mean, then substitute to recover it. The final upper-tail cutoff uses the 95th percentile.
starters.solution:
1. \[95=\mu+\sigma z_{0.10},\qquad107=\mu+\sigma z_{0.75}.\]

    The second cumulative probability is larger, and its measured cutoff is also larger.

  2. \[12=\sigma(z_{0.75}-z_{0.10}),\qquad\sigma=\frac{12}{z_{0.75}-z_{0.10}}\approx6.13.\]

    Both numerator and denominator are positive, so the fitted standard deviation is positive.

  3. \[\mu=95-\sigma z_{0.10}\approx102.86,\qquad\sigma^2\approx37.64.\]

    Using the supplied standard scores gives \(\sigma=\frac{12}{1.956}\) and \(\mu\approx102.86503\), so the supplied-value answer for the mean is \(102.87\), also accepted. Its variance still rounds to \(37.64\). Carry the unrounded standard deviation through both calculations.

  4. \[c=\mu+\sigma z_{0.95}\approx112.95.\]

    Using the supplied standard scores throughout instead gives \(112.96\), also accepted. The cutoff exceeds the mean because its lower-cumulative probability is \(0.95\).

  5. \[P(95<X<107)=0.75-0.10=0.65=\frac{13}{20}.\]

    The probability follows directly from the given cumulative areas. Substituting the unrounded fitted parameters into the first two standardisation equations recovers the required standard scores.

  • 1 mark: form the upper-percentile equation.
  • 1 mark: eliminate the mean by subtraction.

  • 1 mark: square the unrounded standard deviation for the variance.
