sections.title: Which one-observation probability produced the repeated event?
sections.label: Inverse repetition
sections.intro:
Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be independent observations from the same \(\mathrm{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\) model, with positive integer \(n\) and \(\sigma>0\). Write \(F(c)=P(X_i\le c)\). Independence and the common cumulative probability give

\[P(\text{all }n\text{ readings are at most }c)=[F(c)]^n.\]

If this batch probability is \(A\), with \(0<A<1\), recover \(F(c)=A^{\frac{1}{n}}\). If instead the probability of at least one exceedance is \(B\), recover

\[F(c)=(1-B)^{\frac{1}{n}},\qquad c=\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}\!\left((1-B)^{\frac{1}{n}}\right).\]

Complement first when needed, undo the repeated-trial power, then apply the normal inverse. Do not pass the original batch probability directly to the normal inverse.

blocks.html:
Find the cutoff from four independent readings

Each reading follows \(\mathrm{N}(100,225)\). The chance that at least one of the four readings exceeds the cutoff \(c\) is \(0.20\).

  1. The probability all four are at most \(c\) is \(1-0.20=0.80\).
  2. Write \(F(c)=P(X\leq c)\). Independence gives \(F(c)^4=0.80\), so \(F(c)=\sqrt[4]{0.80}\approx0.9457416090\).
  3. Invert the standard normal distribution: \(z=\Phi^{-1}(F(c))\approx1.6048956002\).
  4. Return to the reading scale: \(c=100+15z\approx124.07\). Round after using the unrounded value of \(z\).

The shaded area is the chance of a single reading above \(c\), which is \(1-F(c)\approx0.0543\).

Four independent normal readings with mean one hundred and variance two hundred and twenty-five have a 20% chance of at least one exceedance. The all-below probability is 0.8, the single-reading cumulative probability is its fourth root, and the resulting cutoff is approximately 124.07.

blocks.title: Stop and think: invert the batch event before the normal cutoff
blocks.prompt: Three independent observations each follow \(\mathrm{N}(60,16)\). Their probability of all being at most \(c\) is \(0.729\). Choose the correct calculation order, then find the single-observation lower cumulative probability exactly and the cutoff to two decimal places. For a table method use \(z_{0.90}\approx1.282\).

options.root_first: Take the positive cube root of the batch probability, then use the normal inverse.
options.normal_first: Apply the normal inverse directly to the batch probability.
options.complement_only: Use the complement of the batch probability directly as the normal inverse input.

fields.label: Lower cumulative probability for one observation

blocks.hint: First undo the cube produced by the three independent observations. The normal inverse then uses the recovered one-observation probability, and the standard deviation is four.
blocks.solution:
1. \[[P(X\le c)]^3=0.729,\qquad P(X\le c)=0.9.\]
  2. \[c=60+4z_{0.90}\approx65.12620626\approx65.13.\]

    The supplied quantile gives \(60+4\cdot1.282=65.128\), which also reports \(65.13\).

blocks.html: The inverse step requires a valid probability and identifiable data. For a nondegenerate normal model and a finite positive number of readings, a batch probability exactly zero or one gives no finite cutoff of this form. A power formula also requires the stated independence and common one-observation event probability. Different or dependent readings need a different joint model.

Precision convention. Use an unrounded calculator inverse, or an explicitly supplied intermediate quantile. For the stated table routes, use the supplied three-decimal-place quantile and preserve it through the parameter calculation; checks accept its propagated final rounding. Mixture-count questions supply seven-decimal-place component probabilities and require those values throughout the downstream calculation. Report probabilities to four decimal places and cutoffs or normal parameters to two, unless an exact answer is requested.

sections.title: Is the type chosen anew for each reading or once for the whole batch?
sections.label: Normal mixtures
sections.intro:
If type \(A\) is chosen with probability \(w\) and type \(B\) with probability \(1-w\), find the desired normal area separately within each component. If the component event probabilities are \(q_A\) and \(q_B\), the single-measurement mixture event probability is

\[q=wq_A+(1-w)q_B.\]

This weights areas from disjoint type branches. It does not average normal parameters to create a substitute normal distribution.

blocks.html:
The normal component tail areas give the weighted one-reading chance \(\bar q\approx0.3718\). For four readings, \(P(K\geq1)\approx0.8442\) with fresh choices and \(0.6957\) with one shared choice. Both expected counts are \(4\bar q\approx1.4871\).

The same two component normal areas can produce different four-reading count distributions. Fresh independent type selection uses a binomial model with the weighted one-reading probability; one type shared by the batch uses a weighted mixture of two conditional binomial models.

blocks.title: Distinguish fresh and shared type choices at the batch level
blocks.prompt: Type \(A\) has model \(\mathrm{N}(10,4)\); type \(B\) has model \(\mathrm{N}(14,9)\). Their prior probabilities are \(0.4\) and \(0.6\). A success is a measurement above thirteen. Use the supplied working component probabilities \(q_A=0.0668072\), \(q_B=0.6305587\) throughout. Find the one-measurement mixture probability, then the probability all three measurements succeed when types are chosen independently afresh for each measurement, and when one type is shared by the batch. Measurements are generated independently conditional on their type choices. Give probabilities to four decimal places.

fields.label: All three succeed with fresh independent type choices
All three succeed with one shared type

blocks.hint: For fresh choices, weight the component areas before cubing. For a shared choice, cube within each conditional type first, then weight the branch probabilities.
blocks.solution:
1. \[q=0.4\cdot0.0668072+0.6\cdot0.6305587=0.4050581\approx0.4051.\]
  2. \[P(\text{all three, fresh})\approx(0.4050581)^3\approx0.0665.\]
  3. \[P(\text{all three, shared})\approx0.4\cdot(0.0668072)^3+0.6\cdot(0.6305587)^3\approx0.1505.\]

    The order of weighting and repetition follows the actual type-selection procedure.

blocks.html:
For a shared type and a count of \(r\) successes among \(n\) readings, conditional independence gives

\[P(K=r)=w\binom{n}{r}q_A^r(1-q_A)^{n-r}+(1-w)\binom{n}{r}q_B^r(1-q_B)^{n-r}.\]

For fresh independent type selection on every trial, use \(K\sim\mathrm{B}(n,q)\) with the weighted event probability. These constructions can coincide in special cases, such as identical component event probabilities; the actual procedure determines which expression is justified.

Conditional independence does not automatically give unconditional independence. If one hidden type is shared by the batch, evidence about one reading can change the probabilities for the others. Weight the complete conditional batch events. For a posterior type probability, divide the appropriate type-and-evidence joint probability by the total evidence probability, provided that denominator is positive.

sections.title: Which normal parameter is identified after the batch probability is inverted?
sections.label: Unknown parameters
sections.intro:
Once the repeated-event equation has been reduced to a one-observation condition \(P(X\le a)=\alpha\), use the familiar quantile relation

\[a=\mu+\sigma z_\alpha,\qquad z_\alpha=\Phi^{-1}(\alpha).\]

With known positive standard deviation, solve for the mean. With known mean and nonzero quantile, solve for the standard deviation and require it to be positive. If two distinct compound conditions recover two different percentile levels, form the two corresponding quantile equations and check that their cutoff order is consistent before solving.

blocks.title: Recover a mean from the repeated event’s single-observation percentile
blocks.prompt: Three independent observations each follow \(\mathrm{N}(\mu,9)\). The probability all are below twenty-two is \(0.512\). Find the single-observation lower cumulative probability exactly, and \(\mu\) to two decimal places. For a table method use \(z_{0.80}\approx0.842\).
blocks.hint: The cube root of the batch probability is the single-observation probability. Standardise twenty-two using standard deviation three.
blocks.solution:
1. \[[P(X<22)]^3=0.512,\qquad P(X<22)=0.8,\qquad\frac{22-\mu}{3}=z_{0.80}.\]
  2. \[\mu=22-3z_{0.80}\approx19.47513630\approx19.48.\]

    The supplied table quantile instead gives \(22-3\cdot0.842=19.474\), reporting \(19.47\). Both declared routes are accepted.

blocks.title: Recover a positive spread and recognise an uninformative median condition
blocks.prompt: Two independent observations each follow \(\mathrm{N}(40,\sigma^2)\), with \(\sigma>0\). The probability at least one exceeds forty-five is \(0.36\). Find \(\sigma\) to two decimal places, using a calculator or \(z_{0.80}\approx0.842\). Separately, would knowing only that both observations are below forty with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\) determine \(\sigma\)?

fields.label: Does the separate median-only batch condition determine the spread?

options.no: No: it holds for every positive spread with the stated mean and independence.
options.yes: Yes: the spread must be zero.
options.inconsistent: The stated median-only batch probability is inconsistent.

blocks.hint: The first batch complement is \(0.64\), whose positive square root is the single-observation lower probability \(0.8\). The separate median condition supplies no information about spread.
blocks.solution:
1. \[[P(X\le45)]^2=0.64,\qquad P(X\le45)=0.8,\qquad\sigma=\frac{45-40}{z_{0.80}}\approx5.94.\]

  2. For the separate median-only condition, each observation has probability \(\frac{1}{2}\) of being below forty for every positive standard deviation. Independence gives \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{4}\), regardless of spread.

blocks.html: Check what the event actually identifies. A recovered median condition at the known mean holds for every positive standard deviation. Repeating the same information does not supply an additional independent parameter equation. A negative computed spread or reversed percentile ordering signals inconsistent data or an incorrect event translation; taking an absolute value does not repair it.

Verify the whole chain, not just the last equation. Substitute the recovered parameter into the one-observation normal area, then reconstruct the original batch event using the stated repetition rule. Keep the unrounded parameter for this check and remember that the normal model’s second parameter is the variance.

sections.title: Does an inverse normal-approximation root survive every original restriction?
sections.label: Inverse approximation
sections.intro:
In an inverse binomial approximation, the unknown parameter also appears in the matched normal mean or variance. First translate the discrete event with its continuity correction, then use the lower cumulative quantile. For corrected boundary \(b\), the working equation has the form

\[\frac{b-np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}=z_\alpha.\]

The positive square root, probability domain and sign remain part of this equation. Squaring may create candidates that do not satisfy it. A positive integer is required when the unknown is a trial count, and a probability must lie in its admissible range. The nondegenerate approximation also requires both strict checks \(np>5\) and \(n(1-p)>5\).

blocks.title: Keep the root that satisfies the corrected unsquared equation
blocks.prompt: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(n,\frac{1}{2})\), where \(n\) is a positive integer. Use the prescribed normal-approximation target \(P(X\ge18)\approx1-\Phi(2)\), treating \(z=2\) as the exact working standardised boundary in this approximation. Find the admissible integer candidate and the extraneous candidate obtained by squaring. State whether the retained candidate passes both strict approximation conditions.

fields.label: Squared-equation candidate rejected by the original sign
Do both strict conditions hold for the retained candidate?

options.yes: Yes: both expected counts are twelve and a half, which exceed five.
options.no: No: the first expected count equals five.
options.unchecked: No suitability check is needed after solving an inverse equation.

blocks.hint: The corrected upper-tail event starts at \(17.5\). Its prescribed standardised boundary is positive. Keep that sign condition when squaring the equation.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\frac{17.5-\frac{n}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt{n}}{2}}=2,\qquad\frac{35-n}{\sqrt{n}}=2.\]
  2. \[(35-n)^2=4n,\qquad(n-25)(n-49)=0.\]
  3. \[\frac{35-25}{\sqrt{25}}=2,\qquad\frac{35-49}{\sqrt{49}}=-2.\]

    Retain \(n=25\), reject \(n=49\), and check \(np=n(1-p)=12.5>5\). The retained count is an inverse normal-approximation candidate, not a statement of exact equality for the binomial tail.

blocks.html: Do not accept a root solely because it satisfies the squared polynomial. Substitute every candidate into the original unsquared, continuity-corrected equation. Reject zero denominators, wrong signs, invalid probabilities, impossible event support and noninteger trial counts when the working data require an exact integer solution.

Separate exact working equations from rounded data. The examples prescribe a standardised working target explicitly. If an observed or supplied probability is rounded, a noninteger algebraic estimate does not by itself prove inconsistency: check plausible integer candidates against the original approximation relation at the stated precision. A valid inverse approximation remains an approximation, even after the algebra is exact.

sections.title: Do the recovered parameters define one feasible and informative model chain?
sections.label: Model-chain checks
sections.intro: A model chain can contain several different probabilities: a type prior, a conditional component area, an unconditional event probability, a repeated-event probability and a posterior. Give each its own meaning before combining them. At every step, keep probability values between zero and one, require positive conditioning denominators and standard deviations, and check independence only where the relevant product or binomial formula uses it.

blocks.title: An algebraic mixing weight must still be a probability
blocks.prompt: At a common threshold, two normal component models have exact exceedance probabilities \(q_A=\frac{1}{5}\) and \(q_B=\frac{3}{5}\). Choose type \(A\) with probability \(w\), independently afresh for each measurement, and generate measurements independently given the choices. A proposal claims that at least one of two measurements exceeds the threshold with probability \(0.96\). Recover the implied one-measurement exceedance probability and the algebraic value of \(w\), then decide whether the proposal is feasible.

fields.label: Algebraic value of the type A weight

options.no: No: the required mixing weight is outside the probability range.
options.yes: Yes: any solution of the algebraic equation is a valid mixture.
options.underdetermined: The data are uninformative because both component probabilities are equal.

blocks.hint: Invert the at-least-one formula first. A mixture probability must lie between the two component event probabilities, and a mixing weight must lie between zero and one.
blocks.solution:
1. \[1-(1-q)^2=0.96,\qquad1-q=0.2,\qquad q=0.8=\frac{4}{5}.\]
  2. \[\frac{w}{5}+(1-w)\cdot\frac{3}{5}=\frac{4}{5},\qquad w=-\frac{1}{2}.\]

    The candidate is not a probability. Equivalently, \(\frac{4}{5}\) lies above both component probabilities, so no valid mixture can produce it under the stated independent fresh-choice model.

blocks.html: Feasibility and identifiability are different checks. A mixing weight outside \([0,1]\) is infeasible. An event probability that is identical under both components may be feasible for every weight and therefore identify none. For one event, a mixture probability must lie between its two component probabilities; this provides a useful check before solving for a weight.

Close the model chain with the original event. A final answer should reproduce the stated batch probability under the actual fresh or shared selection procedure, with correct normal tails, continuity boundaries and precision. These methods concern event probabilities and finite counts; they do not assume additional results about normal sums or averages.

glossary.definition: A sequence of explicitly related probability models connecting the original experiment to the requested quantity.
Recovering a one-observation probability from an independent repeated-event probability before using a normal inverse.
An event probability calculated within one specified normal population.
The prior probability of selecting a component population.
Choosing the component independently anew for every measurement.
Choosing one component for a whole batch, with any stated independence applying conditional on that choice.
A type probability updated by dividing its joint probability with the evidence by the total evidence probability.
A candidate introduced by an algebraic transformation that fails the original equation or its domain.
Whether the supplied probability conditions determine the requested parameter uniquely.
Verification that all recovered values and assumptions define an admissible probability model.

examples.title: Invert the repeated event before finding the normal cutoff
examples.question: Four independent readings each follow \(\mathrm{N}(100,225)\). Choose a cutoff \(c\) so that the probability at least one reading exceeds it is \(0.20\). Find \(c\) to two decimal places. Use an unrounded calculator inverse, or the supplied intermediate quantile \(1.604895600\) after deriving the required single-reading cumulative probability.
solution:
Let \(F(c)=P(X\le c)\) for one reading. The complement of at least one exceedance is that all four readings are at most the cutoff. Independence gives

\[1-[F(c)]^4=0.20.\]

Recover the one-reading lower cumulative probability before using the normal inverse:

\[[F(c)]^4=0.80,\qquad F(c)=0.80^{\frac{1}{4}}\approx0.9457416090.\]

The standard deviation is fifteen. Thus

\[\frac{c-100}{15}=\Phi^{-1}\!\left(0.80^{\frac{1}{4}}\right)\approx1.604895600,\]\[c=100+15\Phi^{-1}\!\left(0.80^{\frac{1}{4}}\right)\approx124.0734340\approx124.07.\]

Back-substitute the unrounded cutoff: its one-reading lower probability is approximately \(0.9457416090\), whose fourth power is \(0.80\). The complement is the required \(0.20\). Passing \(0.20\) directly to the normal inverse would invert the batch event as though it described one reading.

examples.title: Weight component areas, then repeat fresh type selections
examples.question: For each measurement independently, choose type \(A\) with probability \(0.6\) or type \(B\) with probability \(0.4\). Type \(A\) measurements follow \(\mathrm{N}(100,225)\); type \(B\) measurements follow \(\mathrm{N}(120,100)\). Measurements are generated independently conditional on their independently chosen types. Find the probability a measurement exceeds one hundred and fifteen, and the probability exactly two of four such measurements do so. Use the supplied component working probabilities \(q_A=0.1586553\) and \(q_B=0.6914625\), retaining them throughout; report probabilities to four decimal places.
solution:
Standardise within each component, using its own mean and standard deviation:

\[q_{A,0}=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{115-100}{15}\right)=1-\Phi(1),\]\[q_{B,0}=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{115-120}{10}\right)=1-\Phi(-0.5).\]

The supplied component probabilities approximate these two areas.

The type branches are disjoint, so weight their event probabilities:

\[q_0=0.6q_{A,0}+0.4q_{B,0}.\]

Using the instructed working probabilities,

\[q\ =0.6\cdot0.1586553+0.4\cdot0.6914625=0.37177818\approx0.3718.\]

Fresh independent type selection and measurement generation on every trial produce independent success indicators with the same unconditional probability. Let \(K\) count the exceedances among the four measurements. Its true count model is \(K\sim\mathrm{B}(4,q_0)\), so

\[P(K=2)=\binom{4}{2}q_0^2(1-q_0)^2\approx\binom{4}{2}(0.37177818)^2(0.62822182)^2\approx0.3273.\]

Averaging the two normal means and variances and treating the result as one normal distribution does not produce this event calculation. A mixture need not be normal; first find each component area, then weight the areas.

examples.title: One shared type creates a mixture of batch-count models
examples.question: Instead, choose one type for the whole four-measurement batch: type \(A\) has prior probability \(0.6\), with measurements from \(\mathrm{N}(100,225)\); type \(B\) has prior probability \(0.4\), with measurements from \(\mathrm{N}(120,100)\). Conditional on the selected type, generate four independent measurements. Let \(K\) count those exceeding one hundred and fifteen. Find the probability all four exceed and the posterior probability that the batch was type \(A\), given all four exceeded. Use \(q_A=0.1586553\), \(q_B=0.6914625\) as working component probabilities throughout. Report probabilities to four decimal places.
solution:
Let \(q_{A,0}\) and \(q_{B,0}\) be the exact within-type exceedance probabilities. Independence is conditional on the shared type. Within each branch, all four exceedances have probability equal to that component probability raised to the fourth power. Weight the complete branch events:

\[P(K=4)=0.6q_{A,0}^4+0.4q_{B,0}^4\approx0.6\cdot(0.1586553)^4+0.4\cdot(0.6914625)^4\approx0.0918.\]

For comparison, fresh type choice on every measurement uses \(q_0=0.6q_{A,0}+0.4q_{B,0}\) and would give

\[P(K=4)=q_0^4\approx(0.37177818)^4\approx0.0191.\]

Both designs have the same one-measurement mixture probability, but they have different batch probabilities because the type-sharing structure differs.

The posterior numerator is the joint probability of choosing type \(A\) and observing all four exceedances. Its denominator includes both possible type branches:

\[P(A\mid K=4)=\frac{0.6q_{A,0}^4}{0.6q_{A,0}^4+0.4q_{B,0}^4}\approx0.0041403134\approx0.0041.\]

The denominator is positive. The evidence strongly favours type \(B\), whose per-measurement exceedance probability is much larger. A shared type does not give the fresh-choice binomial model in this example; the full count distribution is a weighted mixture of the two conditional binomial distributions.

examples.title: Recover an unknown mean from an all-below batch probability
examples.question: Four independent observations each follow \(\mathrm{N}(\mu,16)\). The probability all four are below thirty is \(0.4096\). Find \(\mu\) to two decimal places. For a table method, use \(z_{0.80}\approx0.842\).
solution:
Let \(a=P(X<30)\) for one observation. Independence gives

\[a^4=0.4096,\qquad a=0.8.\]

The nonnegative probability root is required.

The standard deviation is four, so the recovered one-observation condition gives

\[\frac{30-\mu}{4}=z_{0.80}.\]

\[\mu=30-4z_{0.80}\approx26.63351507\approx26.63.\]

The supplied table quantile gives \(\mu\approx30-4\cdot0.842=26.632\), which also reports \(26.63\).

The bound thirty must lie above the recovered mean because its lower cumulative probability is 80%. Back-substitution gives the original single-observation probability \(0.8\), then \((0.8)^4=0.4096\) for the independent batch.

examples.title: Recover a positive spread from a repeated upper-tail event
examples.question: Three independent observations each follow \(\mathrm{N}(50,\sigma^2)\), with \(\sigma>0\). The probability at least one exceeds fifty-six is \(0.488\). Find \(\sigma\) to two decimal places. For a table method, use \(z_{0.80}\approx0.842\).
solution:
Let \(a=P(X\le56)\) for one observation. Complement the repeated upper-tail event:

\[1-a^3=0.488,\qquad a^3=0.512,\qquad a=0.8.\]

The cutoff fifty-six is therefore the 80th percentile of one observation:

\[\frac{56-50}{\sigma}=z_{0.80},\qquad\sigma=\frac{6}{z_{0.80}}.\]

\[\sigma\approx7.129097699\approx7.13.\]

The supplied table value gives \(\sigma\approx\frac{6}{0.842}\approx7.125890736\), also reporting \(7.13\). The positive displacement and positive quantile give the required positive standard deviation.

The second parameter of a reported normal model would be \(\sigma^2\), not \(\sigma\). If a variance is requested, square the unrounded recovered spread. If the recovered cumulative probability had been one half at the known mean, the resulting median condition would not identify the spread.

examples.title: Reject the root introduced by squaring an inverse approximation
examples.question: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(n,\frac{1}{2})\), where \(n\) is an unknown positive integer. An inverse normal-approximation calculation uses the prescribed working target \(P(X\le31)\approx\Phi(2)\). Treat the normal quantile as exactly \(2\) within this approximation calculation; it is not obtained by inverting a rounded percentage. Find a candidate \(n\), check both strict suitability conditions, and reject any root that fails the original corrected equation.
solution:
Match the mean and variance, then apply the continuity correction before solving:

\[Y\sim\mathrm{N}\!\left(\frac{n}{2},\frac{n}{4}\right),\qquad P(X\le31)\approx P(Y<31.5).\]

The prescribed lower-tail target requires

\[\frac{31.5-\frac{n}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt{n}}{2}}=2,\qquad\frac{63-n}{\sqrt{n}}=2.\]

The right side is positive and \(\sqrt{n}>0\), so the original equation requires \(n<63\). Squaring without this sign check produces

\[(63-n)^2=4n,\qquad n^2-130n+3969=0,\]\[(n-49)(n-81)=0.\]

Check both algebraic candidates in the unsquared corrected equation:

\[\frac{63-49}{\sqrt{49}}=2,\qquad\frac{63-81}{\sqrt{81}}=-2.\]

Thus \(n=49\) is retained and \(n=81\) is rejected. The second candidate would match the opposite normal tail.

The retained value is a positive integer, the event is within its possible count range, and

\[np=\frac{49}{2}=24.5>5,\qquad n(1-p)=\frac{49}{2}=24.5>5.\]

The result is the candidate trial number in the prescribed normal-approximation equation. It does not assert that the exact binomial cumulative probability is exactly \(\Phi(2)\). With rounded empirical probabilities, integer candidates must instead be judged at the stated data and approximation precision.

examples.title: A compound probability may contain no information about a mixing weight
examples.question: A batch uses type \(A\) with unknown probability \(w\) and type \(B\) with probability \(1-w\). Type \(A\) has model \(\mathrm{N}(40,4)\); type \(B\) has model \(\mathrm{N}(40,36)\). Choose one type for the batch, then generate three independent readings conditional on that type. The probability at least one reading exceeds forty is \(\frac{7}{8}\). Can this observation determine \(w\)?
solution:
The threshold is the common mean of both normal models. Symmetry therefore gives

\[P(X>40\mid A)=P(X>40\mid B)=\frac{1}{2}.\]

Within either type, the probability at least one of the three readings exceeds the threshold is

\[1-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3=\frac{7}{8}.\]

Weighting the two branch probabilities gives

\[P(\text{at least one exceeds }40)=w\cdot\frac{7}{8}+(1-w)\cdot\frac{7}{8}=\frac{7}{8}\]

for every \(0\le w\le1\). The supplied event probability therefore leaves the mixing weight undetermined.

At this particular threshold, the two component success probabilities coincide. Their conditional count models are both \(\mathrm{B}(3,\frac{1}{2})\), so the shared-type count has that same binomial distribution. This does not make the two underlying normal populations identical, nor does it identify their mixing weight. A second informative threshold or other distinguishing evidence would be needed.

extraPractice.title: Recover a single-event area from an all-success probability
extraPractice.prompt:
Three independent measurements each have model \(X\sim\mathrm{N}(50,16)\). The probability that all three are at most \(c\) is \(0.343\). Find the exact single-measurement probability \(q=P(X\le c)\), the cutoff \(c\), and the exact probability that exactly two of the three are at most \(c\). Supplied standard score: \(z_{0.70}\approx0.524\).

Use a calculator or the supplied three-decimal standard score. Give the cutoff or mean to two decimal places, retaining the chosen score until final rounding. Both stated routes are accepted.

fields.label: Exactly two measurements at most the cutoff

extraPractice.hint: Independence makes the all-three probability \(q^3\). Recover the single-measurement cumulative area before taking an inverse normal value.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[q^3=0.343,\qquad q=0.7=\frac{7}{10}.\]

    The probability-domain solution is used for one observation.

  2. \[\sigma=4,\qquad c=50+4\cdot z_{0.70}\approx52.10.\]

    The cutoff is above the mean because its cumulative area is greater than one half. The supplied score gives the same two-decimal result.

  3. \[P(\text{exactly two})=\binom{3}{2}\cdot\left(\frac{7}{10}\right)^2\cdot\frac{3}{10}=\frac{441}{1000}.\]

    The inverse normal calculation uses the individual probability, whereas the final count uses the three independent threshold outcomes.

extraPractice.title: Reverse an at-least-one event to find an unknown mean
extraPractice.prompt:
Five independent measurements have a common normal distribution with unknown mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(3\). The probability that at least one exceeds \(40\) is \(0.67232\). Find the exact probability that one measurement exceeds \(40\), estimate \(\mu\), and find the exact probability that all five exceed \(40\). Supplied standard score: \(z_{0.80}\approx0.842\).

Use a calculator or the supplied three-decimal standard score. Give the cutoff or mean to two decimal places, retaining the chosen score until final rounding. Both stated routes are accepted.

fields.label: Probability that all five exceed the threshold

extraPractice.hint: First find the probability that no measurement exceeds the threshold. Its fifth root is the individual lower-cumulative area, not the individual upper tail.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[P(\text{none exceeds }40)=1-0.67232=0.32768.\]\[P(X\le40)=(0.32768)^{\frac{1}{5}}=0.8,\qquad P(X>40)=0.2=\frac{1}{5}.\]
  2. \[\frac{40-\mu}{3}=z_{0.80},\qquad\mu=40-3\cdot z_{0.80}\approx37.48.\]

    The supplied score gives \(40-3\cdot0.842=37.474\), which rounds to \(37.47\) and is also accepted. The mean is below the upper-tail cutoff, as required.

  3. \[P(\text{all five exceed }40)=\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^5=\frac{1}{3125}.\]

    This is a different repeated event from at least one exceedance.

extraPractice.title: Recover a mixture weight from a threshold probability
extraPractice.prompt:
A measurement comes from type A with probability \(w\) and type B with probability \(1-w\). Type A has model \(\mathrm{N}(40,16)\); type B has model \(\mathrm{N}(48,16)\). The overall probability of exceeding \(44\) is \(0.60\). For the mixture calculations use the supplied working tail probabilities \(a=0.1586553\) for type A and \(b=0.8413447\) for type B. Find \(w\) and the probability of type B given an exceedance. Could an overall exceedance probability of \(0.90\) be achieved by changing only \(w\) within \([0,1]\)?

Give numerical weights and probabilities to four decimal places, retaining the supplied working values until final rounding.

fields.label: Can changing only the weight give probability 0.90?

options.no: No. A weighted probability must lie between the two component probabilities.
options.yes: Yes. Any probability between zero and one can be obtained by choosing a weight.

extraPractice.hint: Weight the two event probabilities. The mixture weight is itself a probability and must lie between zero and one. For the posterior, divide the type-B-and-exceedance probability by the overall exceedance probability.
extraPractice.solution:
1. The normal standard scores at \(44\) are \(1\) for A and \(-1\) for B, explaining the two supplied tail probabilities. Use

    \[w a+(1-w)b=0.60,\qquad w=\frac{b-0.60}{b-a}\approx0.3535.\]

    This solution lies in the probability domain.

  2. \[P(\mathrm{B}\mid X>44)=\frac{(1-w)b}{0.60}\approx0.9065.\]

    Type B becomes more likely after observing an exceedance because its tail probability is larger.

  3. For \(0\le w\le1\), the weighted tail probability lies between \(a\) and \(b\). Since \(0.90>b\), the proposed alternative is impossible. Averaging the component means or variances is not a replacement for weighting their event probabilities.

extraPractice.title: The time at which the type is chosen changes a batch probability
extraPractice.prompt:
Type C measurements have model \(\mathrm{N}(20,4)\), and type D measurements have model \(\mathrm{N}(24,9)\). The type probabilities are \(\frac{1}{3}\) and \(\frac{2}{3}\). Use the working probabilities \(a=0.1586553\) and \(b=0.7475075\) for exceeding \(22\) under C and D respectively. In the fresh-type procedure, a type is chosen independently before each of three independent measurements. In the shared-type procedure, a type is chosen once for the batch; conditional on that type, the three measurements are independent. Find the single-measurement exceedance probability, the probability that all three exceed \(22\) under each procedure, and the probability that the shared type was D given that all three exceeded \(22\).

Give numerical weights and probabilities to four decimal places, retaining the supplied working values until final rounding.

fields.label: All three exceed under fresh type choices
All three exceed under one shared type
Shared type D given all three exceed

extraPractice.hint: The single-measurement probability is the same weighted average in both procedures. Under fresh independent type choices, multiply that marginal probability across observations. Under a shared type, first calculate the all-three probability within each type, then weight the two cases.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[q=\frac{1}{3}\cdot a+\frac{2}{3}\cdot b\approx0.5512.\]
  2. \[P(\text{all three; fresh})=q^3\approx0.1675.\]

    The fresh type choices and measurements are independent across observations, so their threshold indicators have a common independent probability \(q\).

  3. \[P(\text{all three; shared})=\frac{1}{3}\cdot a^3+\frac{2}{3}\cdot b^3\approx0.2798.\]

    Conditional independence within each chosen type does not make the unconditioned shared-type observations independent.

  4. \[P(\mathrm{D}\mid\text{all three; shared})=\frac{2\cdot b^3}{a^3+2\cdot b^3}\approx0.9952.\]

    The shared type is weighted once for the batch. Multiplying the marginal probability \(q\) three times would use the fresh-type procedure instead.

extraPractice.title: An inverse median condition does not determine spread
extraPractice.prompt: Three independent measurements have common model \(\mathrm{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\), with \(\sigma>0\). The probability that all three are at most \(10\) is \(\frac{1}{8}\). Find \(\mu\), decide whether the standard deviation is uniquely determined, and decide whether the same model can also have probability \(\frac{1}{8}\) that all three are at most \(14\).

fields.label: What is known about the standard deviation?

options.many: Infinitely many positive standard deviations satisfy the first condition.
options.one: Exactly one positive standard deviation is determined.
options.none: No positive standard deviation can satisfy the first condition.

fields.label: Can the second all-three probability also equal one eighth?

options.no: No. Distinct cutoffs cannot have the same normal cumulative probability.
options.yes: Yes. The standard deviation can always be adjusted to satisfy both conditions.

extraPractice.hint: Take the probability-domain cube root first. A normal cumulative probability of one half identifies the mean, but its standard score is zero.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[[P(X\le10)]^3=\frac{1}{8}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad P(X\le10)=\frac{1}{2}.\]\[\frac{10-\mu}{\sigma}=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mu=10.\]

  2. Every positive \(\sigma\) gives the same median \(10\). The equation has a zero standard score, so it supplies no spread information; division by that standard score is not valid.

  3. The proposed additional condition would require \(P(X\le14)=\frac{1}{2}\), which would instead force \(\mu=14\). This contradicts \(\mu=10\). Equivalently, for a positive finite standard deviation the normal cumulative probability strictly increases between distinct cutoffs.

starters.title: Recover a success probability from a signed approximation equation
starters.question: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}(100,p)\), where \(0<p<1\). A continuity-corrected normal approximation is required to give \(P(X\le19)\approx\Phi(1)\). Use the prescribed working standard score \(+1\) exactly in the approximation equation; this avoids inverting a rounded decimal probability. Find the admissible estimate of \(p\), the other candidate produced by squaring, and the resulting normal mean and variance. Select the reason for rejecting the other candidate. Give the two probability candidates to four decimal places and the mean and variance to two decimal places. Check the original signed equation, the parameter domain and both strict suitability conditions.
starters.hint: The corrected boundary is \(19.5\). Before squaring, note the sign of \(19.5-100p\). Squaring loses that sign information, so every algebraic candidate must be substituted into the original equation.
starters.solution:
1. \[\mu=100p,\qquad\sigma^2=100p(1-p),\qquad\frac{19.5-100p}{\sqrt{100p(1-p)}}=1.\]

    The denominator is positive, so the numerator must be positive. Thus an admissible candidate must satisfy \(p<0.195\).

  2. \[(19.5-100p)^2=100p(1-p)\]\[10100p^2-4000p+380.25=0.\]\[p=\frac{4000\pm\sqrt{637900}}{20200}.\]

    The candidates are approximately \(0.1584808702\) and \(0.2375587337\).

  3. The smaller candidate gives corrected standard score \(+1\); the larger gives \(-1\). Therefore the estimate is \(p\approx0.1585\), and \(0.2376\) is rejected. Both lie between zero and one, so the probability domain alone would not remove the extraneous root.

  4. \[\mu=100p\approx15.85,\qquad\sigma^2=100p(1-p)\approx13.34.\]

    These calculations retain the unrounded admissible candidate.

  5. \[np\approx15.8481>5,\qquad n(1-p)\approx84.1519>5.\]

    The strict suitability checks pass. The rejected candidate also passes those checks, but fails the original signed equation. The reported parameter is an estimate obtained from the prescribed normal approximation.

starters.title: Recover an integer trial count and reject a wrong-sign root
starters.question: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{B}\left(n,\frac{1}{4}\right)\), where \(n\) is an unknown positive integer. A continuity-corrected normal approximation is required to give \(P(X\le22)\approx\Phi(1)\). Use the prescribed working standard score \(+1\) exactly in the approximation equation. Find the corrected upper boundary, the admissible trial count, the rejected candidate produced by squaring, and the exact variance and standard deviation of the resulting normal approximation. Show the integer, sign and strict suitability checks.
starters.hint: The normal mean is \(\frac{n}{4}\), variance \(\frac{3n}{16}\), and standard deviation \(\frac{\sqrt{3n}}{4}\). Apply the upper half-unit correction before forming the equation. Its unsquared left side must have the prescribed positive sign.
starters.solution:
1. \[P(X\le22)\approx P(Y<22.5),\qquad Y\sim\mathrm{N}\left(\frac{n}{4},\frac{3n}{16}\right).\]\[\frac{22.5-\frac{n}{4}}{\frac{\sqrt{3n}}{4}}=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad90-n=\sqrt{3n}.\]

    The original equation requires \(n<90\).

  2. \[(90-n)^2=3n\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n^2-183n+8100=0\]\[\Longrightarrow\quad(n-75)(n-108)=0.\]

    Both algebraic candidates are positive integers, so the integer check alone does not choose between them.

  3. For \(n=75\), the signed equation gives \(90-75=15=\sqrt{225}\). For \(n=108\), it would require \(-18=18\), which is false. Hence \(n=75\) is admissible and \(108\) is rejected.

  4. \[np=\frac{75}{4}=18.75>5,\qquad n(1-p)=\frac{225}{4}=56.25>5.\]\[\sigma^2=\frac{3\cdot75}{16}=\frac{225}{16},\qquad\sigma=\frac{15}{4}.\]

    The count cutoff lies inside the binomial support, the trial count is an integer, the standard deviation is positive and both strict suitability checks pass. These are the parameters selected by the prescribed approximation equation.

revision.body:
Keep each probability attached to its own experiment, then work backwards while preserving the model assumptions.

Undo independent repetitions before taking a quantile

For independent measurements from one normal model, write \(F(c)=P(X\le c)\).

\[P(\text{all }n\text{ below }c)=F(c)^n.\]\[P(\text{at least one above }c)=1-F(c)^n.\]

Recover the single-observation cumulative area first. Then use \(z=\Phi^{-1}(F(c))\) and \(c=\mu+\sigma z\), with \(\sigma>0\).

Weight probabilities for a population mixture

\[q=wq_A+(1-w)q_B,\qquad0\le w\le1.\]

The component probabilities refer to the same event. Averaging normal parameters does not generally produce the mixture distribution. A proposed mixture probability must lie between its component probabilities. If \(q_A=q_B\), that event probability cannot identify the weight.

Fresh type choices and one shared type are different experiments

Independent trials, each with a fresh type choice, give \(Y\sim\mathrm{B}(n,q)\). For one shared type, observations are conditionally independent given that type. Calculate the group event \(H\) within each component, then combine:

\[P(H)=wP(H\mid A)+(1-w)P(H\mid B).\]

Both mechanisms have expected count \(nq\), but they can have different count distributions.

Check inverse equations before accepting a candidate

\[x_i=\mu+\sigma z_i,\qquad\frac{b-np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}=z.\]

In an inverse approximation, \(b\) is the continuity-corrected boundary. Test squared roots in the original signed equation. Check positive standard deviation, admissible probabilities, integer trial count and both strict conditions \(np>5\), \(n(1-p)>5\). Substitute into every original condition; retain the prescribed working precision. An approximate model does not make its inferred probability exact.
revision.checks: • Correct experiment and conditioning; independence at the right stage; single-event probability recovered; compatible mixture weights; quantile sign; corrected boundary; original equations and parameter domains; final back-substitution.
